summary: Defines a MIME content type for Message Disposition Notifications, which report what happened to a message after delivery, such as read receipts. It also defines headers for requesting them. It obsoletes RFC 2298, updates RFC 2046 and RFC 3461, was updated by RFC 5337 and RFC 6533, and was replaced by RFC 8098.

plainLanguage.summary: A read receipt tells the sender their mail was opened. This defines the format of those little reports.

questions: what is a message disposition notification
how do email read receipts work
can a recipient refuse a read receipt
subtitle: The standard format for read receipts: how a sender asks for one and how the recipient's mail program reports back.

tldr.problem: Internet mail had no standard, machine-readable way to report what happened to a message after it was delivered, such as that it was displayed, while respecting privacy concerns.
tldr.mechanism: A sender adds a Disposition-Notification-To header to request a report. The recipient's mail program may reply with a multipart/report message containing a message/disposition-notification part of structured fields.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3798 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2298 but has itself been obsoleted by RFC 8098. A request is only a request, and the recipient is free to ignore it.

today: RFC 3798 has been obsoleted by RFC 8098. It obsoleted RFC 2298, updated RFC 2046 and RFC 3461, and was itself updated by RFC 5337 and RFC 6533.

sections.title: What an MDN Is For
sections.content:
A Message Disposition Notification (MDN) tells the sender of a message about something that happened after successful delivery: for example that the message was displayed, printed, or deleted without display, or that the recipient refuses to provide MDNs. The memo defines the message/disposition-notification content type, meant for use inside multipart/report, and the message headers used to request MDNs.

The stated purposes include informing people about message disposition largely independent of human language, letting mail user agents (MUAs) match returned MDNs to earlier messages, and carrying notifications to and from foreign mail systems through gateways. The abstract says the aim is to extend Internet Mail with functions found in X.400 and LAN-based systems, "often referred to as read receipts", while respecting privacy concerns.

The constraints: an MDN must be human-readable and machine-parsable, must let a sender unambiguously tie it to the message and original recipient address, must be independent of any human language, and must be extensible.
sections.plainLanguage: When your letter has been opened, the other person's mailbox can send back a standard little note. The note is written in a fixed way so computers can read it too.

sections.title: Requesting an MDN
sections.content:
A sender asks for an MDN by putting a Disposition-Notification-To header, holding one or more mailboxes, in the message. This is merely a request: recipient user agents are always free to silently ignore it, or to answer with an explicit "denied" disposition.

Rules that limit abuse:

  • An MDN MUST NOT itself carry a Disposition-Notification-To header, and an MDN MUST NOT be generated in response to an MDN.
  • A user agent MUST NOT issue more than one MDN per recipient.
  • It is strongly recommended to get the user's consent before sending an MDN.
  • MDNs SHOULD NOT be sent automatically if the address in Disposition-Notification-To differs from the Return-Path address, if there is no Return-Path, or if there is more than one distinct address. The aim is to reduce mail loops and mail bombing. Messages posted to newsgroups SHOULD NOT carry the header.

Two more headers help. Original-Recipient lets the delivering MTA record the address the sender originally used, since addresses may be rewritten in transit. Disposition-Notification-Options is an extensible list of parameters, each marked required or optional; no parameters are defined in this specification. A sender SHOULD also include a Message-ID so MDNs can be correlated automatically.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask for a receipt, but the other person can always say no or ignore you. Rules also stop a receipt from triggering another receipt, which would go on forever.

sections.title: Format of an MDN
sections.content:
An MDN is a MIME message whose top-level type is multipart/report with the report-type parameter disposition-notification. It has up to three parts: a human-readable explanation, a message/disposition-notification part with the structured fields, and optionally the original message or a portion of it. Encrypted message text MUST be returned only in its original encrypted form, if returned at all.

The MDN MUST be addressed, in the header and the transport envelope, to the addresses in the original Disposition-Notification-To header. Its envelope sender (SMTP MAIL FROM) MUST be null (<>) so no delivery status notifications come back about it. One MDN describes exactly one message for exactly one recipient.

The RFC gives an illustrative example, reproduced in the viz below, issued after a message was displayed.
sections.plainLanguage: The receipt is a small envelope with three pages: a note a person can read, a form a computer can read, and maybe a copy of your original letter.

sections.title: The Report Fields and Dispositions
sections.content:
The machine-readable part is a list of fields in message-header style. Required: Final-Recipient (the recipient the MDN is for) and Disposition. Optional: Reporting-UA (the MUA that acted), MDN-Gateway (present only if a gateway translated a foreign notification), Original-Recipient, Original-Message-ID (MUST be present if the original had a Message-ID), plus Failure, Error, Warning and extension fields.

The Disposition field combines a mode with a type. The action mode is manual-action or automatic-action, and the sending mode is MDN-sent-manually or MDN-sent-automatically; exactly one of each pair MUST be given. The disposition types defined here are displayed and deleted. The RFC stresses that "displayed" is no guarantee that the content was read or understood, and a "deleted" message may be undeleted and read later. Names not starting with X- must be registered with IANA, while X- names are reserved for experimental use.
sections.plainLanguage: The form says who the receipt is for and what happened, such as opened or thrown away. It also says whether a person pressed a button or a program did it on its own.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC lists four concerns. Forgery: MDNs can be forged as easily as ordinary mail, so automatic users should limit damage from denial-of-service. Privacy: a recipient may not want to reveal when a message was read, so it is acceptable to issue "denied" MDNs or ignore requests. Passing the request unchanged to a mailing list could reveal subscribers, and returning headers could reveal host names or network topology behind a firewall. Encrypted MDNs are not defined.

Non-repudiation: MDNs do not give proof of delivery and cannot be relied on as a guarantee that a message was or was not seen, since they may be lost or bypassed. Mail bombing: an attacker could send many messages with a false notification address, so MDNs SHOULD NOT be sent automatically when that address differs from the envelope MAIL FROM address.
sections.plainLanguage: A receipt can be faked, can tell on you for reading something, and cannot prove anything. So mail programs should be careful about sending them automatically.

sections.title: Gateways and Changes From RFC 2298
sections.content:
Non-binding guidelines cover gateways between Internet mail and other systems. A gateway turning a foreign notification into an MDN must put its name in the MDN-Gateway field and try to give sensible values for Reporting-UA, Final-Recipient and Disposition. Foreign data with no MDN equivalent can travel in extension fields. An MDN request whose notification address differs from the SMTP MAIL FROM address should be silently dropped when gatewayed to a system without a separate notification address.

Appendix A lists changes from RFC 2298: new editors, the "denied" and "failed" dispositions removed for lack of implementation or usage, the "warning", "superseded", "expired" and "mailbox-terminated" modifiers removed, and a simplified notification-options grammar.
sections.plainLanguage: Other mail systems have their own kinds of receipts. A gateway translates between them, and it has to sign its name when it does.
